# Pitch Deck Review: Acmecorp

**Date:** 2026-10-24 | **Slides:** 6 | **Format:** text  
**Generated by:** [founder skills](https://github.com/lool-ventures/founder-skills) by [lool ventures](https://lool.vc) — Deck Review Agent

## Executive Summary

**Stage:** Seed (confidence: high)
**Slide Count:** 6
**Deck-craft score:** 25.9% — Major Revision — worth reworking before it goes out; see the fixes below
**Breakdown:** 2 pass, 16 fail, 11 warn, 5 N/A

*Those 16 failures fall into 6 areas, not 16 separate problems — the largest is **Slide Content** (7). Fixing an area usually closes several at once.*

*Score = (pass + half credit per warn) ÷ applicable. Measures conformance to 34 scored deck-craft criteria, not investability.*

**On the AI criteria:** this deck claims AI without showing AI at its core, so the four AI criteria are scored rather than set aside — claiming it invites the bar.

*Why: Deck tagline states 'AI-native developer tools'; no evidence of ML in value prop, inference/training in COGS, foundation-model mentions, or AI-specific retention metrics*

*If that reading is wrong — the product genuinely is AI-native, or the deck never meant to claim it — tell me and those four come out of the score.*

> **4 design criteria could not be reviewed.** This deck reached the review as text — its slides were never rendered, so nothing here judges how the deck *looks*: layout, typography, whitespace, or how it reads on a phone. Sending the deck as a PDF gets them reviewed. Those criteria are excluded from the score rather than counted against you.

> **What this review does not cover.** These 34 scored criteria assess how the deck is built — story, evidence, structure. They do not assess your market, your technology, or the regulatory, clinical, licensing or compliance questions specific to your sector. An investor will ask about those separately, and a clean score here is not evidence they are handled.

## Coaching Commentary

This deck would not get a first meeting in its current state — but it should, and the gap is fixable. The traction is real: $8K MRR, 24 paying customers, and 18% month-over-month growth over four months is a genuine signal for a seed-stage developer tool. That number belongs at the top of every investor conversation. What most hurts is not any single missing slide — it is that the deck has only six slides, each containing 9–23 words of substantive content, and an investor reading it without narration would come away with almost no information on which to base a decision. The deck is a skeleton, not a story. Add the body, and the traction alone could carry a meeting.

**What you should feel good about**

Your traction slide is the strongest thing in the deck, and it is doing real work. $8K MRR with 24 paying customers means your average customer is paying roughly $333 per month — a healthy ARPU for a developer tool at this stage. The 18% month-over-month growth rate over four months is the kind of number that makes investors lean forward. The problem slide also names a specific user (indie SaaS founders) and puts a concrete number on their pain (20+ hours per week on tooling integration), which meets the core Sequoia requirement for a problem statement. And the founding team's background — ex-Stripe engineering, ex-Notion product — is directly relevant to what you are building; you have used the exact stack Acmecorp replaces.

**The single highest-leverage change**

Before anything else, add contact information to the title slide. This costs nothing, takes five minutes, and is the one fix that has immediate impact: DocSend data shows investors often jump directly to contact after reviewing traction, and a deck with no email, no URL, and no presenter name creates friction at exactly the moment of highest interest. Do this today.

The higher-order problem is content density. The six existing slides form the right skeleton — problem, solution, traction, team, ask — but six sections is roughly half what a seed deck needs, and each existing slide needs to be expanded so it can stand alone. The deck is missing: a why-now slide, a market-sizing slide (the opportunity size is never mentioned), a competition slide (absent, which signals avoidance rather than confidence), a business model slide (you have $8K MRR but no explanation of how you charge or what your margins are), a go-to-market slide (how did you get the first 24 customers?), and financial projections. Sequoia, DocSend, and YC all treat these as required at seed; investors reading a six-slide deck with no market size and no competitive landscape will not move forward.

The solution slide is the most urgent individual fix after the contact information. It currently describes the product form factor ("wraps GitHub, Linear, Stripe, and Vercel into one CLI") but never closes the loop the problem slide opened. Show what changes: how many hours does the CLI save per week? What does an indie SaaS founder stop doing, and what do they do instead? Add a CLI screenshot or a three-line command example. The problem slide established the pain; the solution slide should show the relief, not the packaging.

**Would an investor take the meeting?**

Not from this deck as sent, but yes from the underlying company with a fuller deck. The traction is the reason. An investor who heard the numbers — $8K MRR, 24 customers, 18% MoM growth, four months — and then saw a deck that explained the market, the competitive positioning, the business model, and the path from here to $50K MRR, would have a reasonable basis for a seed meeting. The deck's current problem is that it does not let the traction do that work: it states the numbers in a single text line and then moves on, with no chart, no cohort view, no retention data, and no financial model connecting the raise to a milestone. YC's ask-slide guidance is explicit — investors want to know what the company will achieve with the money, not just how long the money will last — and the current three-runway-scenario structure reads as milestone planning that has not been done yet.

**The AI-native claim needs to be resolved**

This is the deck's most immediate credibility risk. The title slide positions Acmecorp as "AI-native developer tools" but no slide in the deck substantiates that claim — no model, no inference, no AI-specific capability appears anywhere. YC partners have noted that unsubstantiated AI claims invite hard technical questions in the first meeting, and a16z flags API wrappers without a stated moat as not defensible. The fix is binary: either remove "AI-native" from the tagline and describe the product accurately (a powerful CLI for the indie SaaS stack), or add a slide showing specifically what the AI does, what data it processes, and what outcome it delivers that a non-AI CLI cannot match. An unsubstantiated AI label is more damaging than no AI claim at all.

**A note on the design assessment**

Four visual design criteria — covering layout, type, color, and slide density — could not be assessed because the deck reached this review as text rather than as a rendered file. This is a gap in the review, not a strength or a criticism of the deck's look. If you would like those criteria scored, share a PDF export and the design section can be completed.

**Narrative and positioning**

The current positioning targets indie SaaS founders specifically, which is a strength — a defined ICP is more credible than "developers" broadly. The competitive question an investor will ask immediately is: what prevents GitHub, Stripe, or Vercel from building this themselves? The deck has no answer. A defensibility section — workflow data accumulated as founders use the CLI, switching cost once it is embedded in daily CI/CD and billing workflows, or vertical specialization that a general-purpose tool cannot match — is not optional at seed for a product in this space. Build that argument before the first investor meeting, whether or not it ends up as its own slide.

The ask also needs to commit. Three raise options ($1.0M / 14 months, $1.5M / 20 months, $2.0M / 26 months) communicates that the founders have not yet decided what they are building toward. Pick one number — the 2025/2026 seed median is roughly $3.8M, and the $1.0M option sits in pre-seed territory — state the specific milestone it buys (a target MRR, a customer count, a repeatable growth motion by a named date), and show a simple use-of-funds breakdown. Confidence in the ask is itself a signal investors read.
## Stage Context

**Detected Stage:** Seed

**Evidence:**
- $8K MRR with 24 paying customers indicates real demand beyond idea/prototype stage
- 18% MoM growth over 4 months shows consistent acquisition motion
- Ask of $1.0M-$2.0M is at the lower end of seed range (though upper pre-seed)
- Product in production integrating four major tools (GitHub, Linear, Stripe, Vercel)

**Typical Round Size:** $2M–$6M (median ~$3.8M for seed; $1M-2M is at lower/pre-seed end)
**Expected Traction:** $300K–$500K ARR signal increasingly expected; $8K MRR ($96K ARR) is early
**Runway Expectation:** 18–24 months minimum (seed-to-A stretches 3+ years)

*Stage benchmarks are reference data from industry standards (Sequoia, DocSend, YC, a16z, Carta). They represent typical ranges, not recommendations.*

## Slide-by-Slide Feedback

*Each slide assessment is the agent's evaluation against best-practice frameworks. Strengths and weaknesses are the agent's analysis, not investor quotes.*

### Slide 1: "Acmecorp — AI-native developer tools for indie SaaS founders" (Purpose/title slide)

**What's working:**
- Names a specific customer segment ('indie SaaS founders') rather than a generic audience, which immediately signals market focus — Sequoia recommends defining the company in a single declarative sentence that names who it serves.
- The category ('developer tools') is stated plainly, so an investor reading at speed knows the space without additional context.
**What investors will question:**
- The 'AI-native' claim in the tagline is not substantiated anywhere in the deck. Deck-inventory evidence shows no ML in the value prop, no inference or training in COGS, no foundation-model mentions, and no AI-specific retention metrics — the label is a positioning choice with no backing, which investors with technical advisors will probe immediately.
- No contact information, website, or presenter name appears. DocSend data shows investors spend an average of 2:30 on a deck and often jump directly to contact after traction; a missing contact block adds friction at the moment of highest intent.
- The tagline describes what the product is ('developer tools') but not what it does or what it changes — Sequoia's pitch framework asks for a single sentence that captures the company's purpose, not its category.
  *Principles: Sequoia: define the company in a single declarative sentence, DocSend: investors spend an average of 2:30 on a deck; contact info must be immediately findable, YC: unsubstantiated AI claims invite hard technical scrutiny in the first meeting*

**How to fix:**
- Either substantiate the 'AI-native' claim in the solution or traction slides (showing how AI is core to the product's value delivery, not just a marketing label) or remove it from the tagline. YC partners have noted that unsubstantiated AI claims invite hard technical questions in the first meeting.
- Add a contact block (email, website, LinkedIn) and the presenter's name to the title slide.
- Rewrite the tagline as a value-proposition sentence: what does Acmecorp do, for whom, and what changes as a result? Example structure: 'Acmecorp gives indie SaaS founders one CLI that replaces the 20+ hours a week they spend stitching together GitHub, Linear, Stripe, and Vercel.'

### Slide 2: "Problem: 20+ hours/week wasted on developer tooling integration" (Problem with quantified pain)

**What's working:**
- Pain is quantified ('20+ hours/week') and tied to a specific customer type (indie SaaS founders), which is exactly what Sequoia's problem-slide guidance calls for: a concrete, measurable cost the customer is already paying.
- The named customer segment (indie SaaS founders) is narrow enough to be credible and large enough to be interesting as a beachhead.
**What investors will question:**
- No source is cited for the '20+ hours/week' figure. YC advisors consistently flag unsourced pain quantifications as a red flag: investors ask 'how do you know?' and a verbal answer in the meeting is weaker than a slide that shows the research.
- The slide contains a single sentence with no supporting evidence — no customer quotes, no survey data, no anecdotes. a16z's pitch-deck guidance notes that a problem slide without customer discovery evidence reads as a hypothesis, not a finding.
- The problem is described at the category level ('developer tooling integration') without showing what the experience of that pain looks like day-to-day. Investors respond more strongly to a concrete scenario than to an abstraction.
  *Principles: Sequoia: problem slides should quantify the cost in concrete, measurable terms, YC: unsourced pain quantifications invite immediate pushback in meetings, a16z: customer discovery evidence on the problem slide turns a hypothesis into a finding, DocSend: social proof on the problem slide increases time-on-slide*

**How to fix:**
- Add a source for the '20+ hours/week' figure — a customer survey, a specific interview quote, or a public benchmark. If it comes from your own users, say so: '8 of our 24 paying customers reported spending 20+ hours/week before Acmecorp' is both more credible and more specific.
- Include one or two direct customer quotes (first name and company type is sufficient) that describe the frustration in their own words. DocSend research shows that decks with social proof on the problem slide hold investor attention longer.
- Show the concrete failure mode: what does a founder actually have to do today — manually copying deploy logs, switching between four dashboards, writing glue scripts — so the investor feels the pain before seeing the solution.

### Slide 3: "Solution: One CLI wrapping GitHub, Linear, Stripe, and Vercel" (Solution (workflow change))

**What's working:**
- The solution is described concretely: four specific tools are named (GitHub, Linear, Stripe, Vercel), which signals the founders know the technical stack their customers use rather than speaking in abstractions.
- A CLI is a credible delivery mechanism for a developer-tools product — it fits the customer's existing workflow, which Sequoia's solution-slide framework calls 'meeting the customer where they are.'
**What investors will question:**
- The slide describes what the product IS ('one CLI') but not what it DOES differently or how it changes the workflow. Sequoia and YC both emphasize that a solution slide should show the before/after transformation, not just the product form factor.
- No screenshot, demo, or workflow diagram is present. a16z's deck guidance notes that developer-tool pitches without a visual of the product (even a CLI screenshot) leave investors uncertain whether the product exists.
- The connection between the problem (20+ hours/week wasted) and this solution (one CLI) is never made explicit. How much time does Acmecorp save? What does the workflow look like after? The slide leaves the investor to infer.
- No explanation of the AI-native claim from Slide 1: if AI is core to how the CLI works, this is where it should be shown.
  *Principles: Sequoia: solution slides should show the workflow change, not just the product form factor, YC: developer-tool decks without a product visual raise questions about product maturity, a16z: the solution slide should close the loop with the problem's quantified pain*

**How to fix:**
- Add a before/after workflow comparison: what does the indie SaaS founder do today across four tools (n steps, n minutes), and what does the Acmecorp CLI reduce that to? Sequoia recommends showing the workflow change, not just the product.
- Include a short CLI screenshot or a three-line demo showing a real command and its output. YC partners note that developer-tool decks with no product visual make investors wonder if there is a product to show.
- Explicitly close the loop with the problem: 'Acmecorp cuts integration overhead from 20+ hours/week to under 2' (or whatever the real figure is) — quantify the solution the same way the problem was quantified.
- If AI drives any part of the product (routing, synthesis, automation), show it here with one concrete example.

### Slide 4: "Traction: $8K MRR, 24 paying customers, 18% MoM growth" (Traction (MRR, growth, cohort data))

**What's working:**
- Three concrete metrics are present: '$8K MRR, 24 paying customers, 18% MoM growth (last 4 months).' Paying customers with real MRR is the most credible traction signal at seed stage — Carta's seed-stage data shows that decks with MRR over $5K attract significantly more investor meetings than those showing only pilots or LOIs.
- 18% MoM growth over four months is strong: it annualizes to roughly 7x revenue growth, and DocSend research identifies growth rate as the metric investors spend the most time on in traction slides.
- The four-month window is honestly labeled, which signals founder credibility — no attempt to obscure a short track record.
**What investors will question:**
- No growth chart is present. DocSend data shows investors spend 88% more time on traction slides that include a visual chart versus those that present only numbers. A single line of text carrying three metrics is the weakest possible format for the deck's most important data.
- No retention or churn data. At seed stage, a16z's framework asks: 'Are customers staying?' 18% MoM growth means little if churn is 15% MoM. Even a simple 'net revenue retention > 100%' or 'zero churn in four months' sentence would address this.
- No customer names or logos (even anonymized by type: 'early-stage SaaS, Series A SaaS, bootstrapped'). DocSend shows that named or typed customer references significantly increase investor confidence in the paying-customer count.
- ARR is not stated. Investors think in ARR for SaaS; $8K MRR = ~$96K ARR and should be stated explicitly so the investor does not have to calculate it.
- No cohort data. The stage profile's expected framework lists cohort data as expected at seed stage, and its absence means an investor cannot assess whether the growth is improving or degrading.
  *Principles: DocSend: investors spend 88% more time on traction slides with visual charts; growth rate is the most-examined metric, a16z: seed-stage traction slides should answer both growth rate and retention, Carta: decks with MRR over $5K attract significantly more seed investor meetings than those showing pilots or LOIs*

**How to fix:**
- Replace the single text line with an MRR growth chart covering the four available months. Label each data point. This is the single highest-leverage visual change in the deck — DocSend's data on investor attention makes this a near-certain improvement.
- Add a retention statement: either net revenue retention, monthly churn rate, or a direct statement that no customer has churned in the four months of operation.
- State ARR explicitly: '$8K MRR ($96K ARR)' removes a calculation the investor should not have to do.
- If customers can be named (even by type), include a two-line customer bar. If not, describe the customer profile: 'customers are bootstrapped and early-stage SaaS founders with $10K–$200K ARR of their own.'

### Slide 5: "Team: 2 co-founders, ex-Stripe and ex-Notion" (Team)

**What's working:**
- Ex-Stripe (engineering) and ex-Notion (product) backgrounds are directly relevant to a developer-tools product aimed at SaaS builders — both companies are in the exact stack Acmecorp integrates. Sequoia's team-slide framework specifically values prior-company relevance over prestige.
- The engineering/product split is the canonical co-founder pairing for a technical B2B product, which a16z research shows is the most fundable founding team structure for developer tools.
**What investors will question:**
- No names are given. Investors routinely Google founders during or immediately after a pitch; a nameless team slide makes that impossible and signals low confidence. YC's application guidance treats named founders as a baseline requirement.
- No specifics about what each founder built at Stripe or Notion. 'Ex-Stripe (eng)' could mean anything from a junior engineer to a founding team member. The specific project, scale, or responsibility is what makes the background credible rather than merely notable.
- Only two people are listed with no detail. No advisors, no third team member, no note about plans to hire. Investors ask 'can this team execute the GTM and technical roadmap?' and two lines of text cannot answer it.
- No LinkedIn or GitHub links for independent verification.
  *Principles: Sequoia: team slides should show relevant execution, not just prestigious employers, YC: named, verifiable founders are a baseline requirement for a credible team slide, a16z: engineering/product co-founder split is the most fundable structure for developer-tool companies*

**How to fix:**
- Add full names and titles for both founders. This is a baseline requirement — YC and Sequoia both treat named, verifiable founders as a minimum for a credible team slide.
- Add one specific achievement at each prior company: 'Built Stripe's developer-dashboard SDK (used by 50K+ developers)' is worth ten times 'ex-Stripe (eng).' Sequoia's team framework calls this 'proof of relevant execution.'
- Consider adding one or two advisors with specific roles — an investor-facing advisor, a domain-expert advisor in developer tooling — to show the founders are building a support network.
- If either founder has shipped open-source projects or developer tools used by the target audience, name them: it is the most direct evidence of founder-market fit for this product.

### Slide 6: "Ask: $1.0M–$2.0M raise with three runway scenarios" (Ask with milestone plan)

**What's working:**
- Three raise options with explicit runway projections ($1.0M / 14 months, $1.5M / 20 months, $2.0M / 26 months) show the founders have done the math and can articulate the relationship between capital and time — which Sequoia's ask-slide guidance cites as a minimum requirement.
- Stating a range rather than a single number can open conversation about what the investor can lead, though it also carries risks (see weaknesses).
**What investors will question:**
- Presenting three options signals uncertainty about what the company actually needs, which a16z and Sequoia both flag as a red flag: a founder who does not know how much they need has not yet done the milestone planning that justifies the ask.
- No milestone plan is included. YC's ask-slide guidance is explicit: investors want to know what the company will achieve with the money, not just how long it will last. '14 months of runway' is a time statement, not a plan.
- No use-of-funds breakdown. Carta's fundraising data shows that asks with a use-of-funds breakdown (even high-level: 'X% engineering, Y% GTM') increase investor confidence in the team's operational planning.
- All three runway options are below the seed-stage benchmark. The stage profile notes a minimum expectation of 18–24 months; the $1.0M option at 14 months is materially below that threshold, and even the $2.0M option at 26 months sits at the low end. Raising at the low end of seed with below-benchmark runway raises questions about whether the round is sized for the stage.
- The implied burn rate from the three options (approximately $71K–$77K per month) is never explained or connected to a hiring or product plan.
  *Principles: Sequoia: the ask slide should name the milestone the capital is buying, not just the runway it funds, YC: three raise options signal the founder has not completed milestone planning, a16z: a single committed ask with a rationale outperforms a range in investor meetings, Carta: use-of-funds breakdowns on the ask slide are correlated with higher investor confidence*

**How to fix:**
- Commit to one ask amount and explain why. The canonical Sequoia structure: 'We are raising $X to [specific milestone — e.g., reach $50K MRR, hire two engineers, sign three enterprise pilots] by [date].' The milestone, not the runway, is what justifies the raise.
- Add a use-of-funds breakdown: even three buckets (engineering, GTM, operations) with percentages shows operational intent. Carta's data links this directly to investor confidence.
- Target at least $1.5M–$2.0M to reach the 18-month minimum runway benchmark the stage profile identifies, and consider whether a $2M–$3M seed is more appropriate given the stage expectations ($2M–$6M median).
- Add a milestone slide or a milestone section on this slide: 'With $2.0M we will reach $50K MRR, 200 paying customers, and a repeatable PLG motion by Q4 2027' — this is what YC means by an ask that tells investors what they are buying.

### Slides to Add

Investors at your stage will expect these:

- **[Critical]** Market (TAM/SAM/SOM): Add a market-sizing slide showing TAM, SAM, and SOM for the indie SaaS developer-tools market. Sequoia and a16z both treat market size as a required slide at seed: investors need to see that the opportunity is large enough to return the fund. Bottom-up sizing (number of indie SaaS founders × average tool spend) is more credible than top-down research citations.
- **[Critical]** Competition/alternatives: Add a competitive landscape slide mapping how Acmecorp differs from existing alternatives (individual tool CLIs, all-in-one platforms like Railway or Render, custom scripts). DocSend data shows that decks without a competition slide rank lower in investor scoring, because the absence suggests the founder either has not done the research or is avoiding a difficult conversation. The goal is not to dismiss competitors but to show why this team wins.
- **[Important]** Business model: Add a business model slide showing pricing, contract structure, and unit economics. At seed stage, investors expect to see the per-seat or usage-based pricing model, the ARPU implied by $8K MRR across 24 customers (~$333/month average), and the path to expansion revenue. Carta's seed-benchmark data identifies missing business model slides as one of the top reasons a deck does not advance to a partner meeting.
- **[Important]** Go-to-market: Add a GTM slide explaining how Acmecorp acquires customers. At seed, investors want to see the acquisition motion — community-led, product-led, content-led, or direct outreach — and early evidence that it works. 24 paying customers acquired through a documented motion is a much stronger signal than 24 customers whose origin is unexplained. YC specifically asks 'how will you get your first 1,000 customers?' and expects an answer in the deck.
- **[Important]** Financials / projections: Add an 18–24 month financial projection slide showing the revenue, headcount, and burn trajectory. This is where the ask connects to the milestone: if the company is raising $2.0M, investors expect to see what that capital buys in MRR, customer count, and team size over the runway period. The projection does not need to be precise — it needs to show that the founders have a model.
- **[Nice to have]** Why now: Consider adding a 'why now' slide explaining what has changed in the environment that makes this the right moment to build Acmecorp. At seed stage this is optional but powerful: the rise of indie SaaS as a category, the proliferation of tools in the developer stack, or a specific platform shift (e.g., AI-assisted coding increasing the number of solo developers) would all strengthen the narrative. Sequoia's pitch framework lists 'why now' as a slide that separates a good story from a great one.

### Overall Narrative

The deck traces a coherent arc from problem to solution to traction to ask, which is the right skeleton — but at six slides with a combined word count well under 100 words of substantive content, it is a skeleton and nothing more. The traction numbers ($8K MRR, 18% MoM growth, 24 paying customers) are the deck's genuine strength and deserve to be the centerpiece of a much richer story; instead, they are presented in a single sentence with no chart, no context, and no retention data. Three critical slides are entirely absent (market, competition, business model), and the ask slide's three-option structure signals that the founders have not yet done the milestone planning investors are purchasing. The 'AI-native' claim in the title is unsubstantiated anywhere in the six slides, which creates a credibility risk with technically sophisticated investors. For a seed round, the deck needs to be rebuilt with full sections on market sizing, competitive differentiation, and GTM, and the existing traction slide needs a growth chart and retention data as its foundation. The founders have real signal to show — the task is building a deck that does justice to it.


## What Your Numbers Say About Each Other

- **Why-now has genuine macro catalyst** (Slide Content)

This deck would not get a first meeting in its current state — but it should, and the gap is fixable. The traction is real: $8K MRR, 24 paying customers, and 18% month-over-month growth over four months is a genuine signal for a seed-stage developer tool. That number belongs at the top of every investor conversation. What most hurts is not any single missing slide — it is that the deck has only six slides, each containing 9–23 words of substantive content, and an investor reading it without narration would come away with almost no information on which to base a decision. The deck is a skeleton, not a story. Add the body, and the traction alone could carry a meeting.

**What you should feel good about**

Your traction slide is the strongest thing in the deck, and it is doing real work. $8K MRR with 24 paying customers means your average customer is paying roughly $333 per month — a healthy ARPU for a developer tool at this stage. The 18% month-over-month growth rate over four months is the kind of number that makes investors lean forward. The problem slide also names a specific user (indie SaaS founders) and puts a concrete number on their pain (20+ hours per week on tooling integration), which meets the core Sequoia requirement for a problem statement. And the founding team's background — ex-Stripe engineering, ex-Notion product — is directly relevant to what you are building; you have used the exact stack Acmecorp replaces.

**The single highest-leverage change**

Before anything else, add contact information to the title slide. This costs nothing, takes five minutes, and is the one fix that has immediate impact: DocSend data shows investors often jump directly to contact after reviewing traction, and a deck with no email, no URL, and no presenter name creates friction at exactly the moment of highest interest. Do this today.

The higher-order problem is content density. The six existing slides form the right skeleton — problem, solution, traction, team, ask — but six sections is roughly half what a seed deck needs, and each existing slide needs to be expanded so it can stand alone. The deck is missing: a why-now slide, a market-sizing slide (the opportunity size is never mentioned), a competition slide (absent, which signals avoidance rather than confidence), a business model slide (you have $8K MRR but no explanation of how you charge or what your margins are), a go-to-market slide (how did you get the first 24 customers?), and financial projections. Sequoia, DocSend, and YC all treat these as required at seed; investors reading a six-slide deck with no market size and no competitive landscape will not move forward.

The solution slide is the most urgent individual fix after the contact information. It currently describes the product form factor ("wraps GitHub, Linear, Stripe, and Vercel into one CLI") but never closes the loop the problem slide opened. Show what changes: how many hours does the CLI save per week? What does an indie SaaS founder stop doing, and what do they do instead? Add a CLI screenshot or a three-line command example. The problem slide established the pain; the solution slide should show the relief, not the packaging.

**Would an investor take the meeting?**

Not from this deck as sent, but yes from the underlying company with a fuller deck. The traction is the reason. An investor who heard the numbers — $8K MRR, 24 customers, 18% MoM growth, four months — and then saw a deck that explained the market, the competitive positioning, the business model, and the path from here to $50K MRR, would have a reasonable basis for a seed meeting. The deck's current problem is that it does not let the traction do that work: it states the numbers in a single text line and then moves on, with no chart, no cohort view, no retention data, and no financial model connecting the raise to a milestone. YC's ask-slide guidance is explicit — investors want to know what the company will achieve with the money, not just how long the money will last — and the current three-runway-scenario structure reads as milestone planning that has not been done yet.

**The AI-native claim needs to be resolved**

This is the deck's most immediate credibility risk. The title slide positions Acmecorp as "AI-native developer tools" but no slide in the deck substantiates that claim — no model, no inference, no AI-specific capability appears anywhere. YC partners have noted that unsubstantiated AI claims invite hard technical questions in the first meeting, and a16z flags API wrappers without a stated moat as not defensible. The fix is binary: either remove "AI-native" from the tagline and describe the product accurately (a powerful CLI for the indie SaaS stack), or add a slide showing specifically what the AI does, what data it processes, and what outcome it delivers that a non-AI CLI cannot match. An unsubstantiated AI label is more damaging than no AI claim at all.

**A note on the design assessment**

Four visual design criteria — covering layout, type, color, and slide density — could not be assessed because the deck reached this review as text rather than as a rendered file. This is a gap in the review, not a strength or a criticism of the deck's look. If you would like those criteria scored, share a PDF export and the design section can be completed.

**Narrative and positioning**

The current positioning targets indie SaaS founders specifically, which is a strength — a defined ICP is more credible than "developers" broadly. The competitive question an investor will ask immediately is: what prevents GitHub, Stripe, or Vercel from building this themselves? The deck has no answer. A defensibility section — workflow data accumulated as founders use the CLI, switching cost once it is embedded in daily CI/CD and billing workflows, or vertical specialization that a general-purpose tool cannot match — is not optional at seed for a product in this space. Build that argument before the first investor meeting, whether or not it ends up as its own slide.

The ask also needs to commit. Three raise options ($1.0M / 14 months, $1.5M / 20 months, $2.0M / 26 months) communicates that the founders have not yet decided what they are building toward. Pick one number — the 2025/2026 seed median is roughly $3.8M, and the $1.0M option sits in pre-seed territory — state the specific milestone it buys (a target MRR, a customer count, a repeatable growth motion by a named date), and show a simple use-of-funds breakdown. Confidence in the ask is itself a signal investors read.
